title: Parity and invariants
objectives: Solve a problem by finding a quantity that never changes.
Tell an invariant, which rules a target out, from a construction, which reaches it.

explain.text: However you played, the six never met in one box. Nine positions can be reached from 3, 2, 1, and none has all six together. Next we find out why without trying every move.

screens.title: What never changes
screens.prose: These are all nine positions you can reach from 3, 2, 1. Look for a quantity that is the same in every row but differs when all six tokens share a box.
screens.question: Which quantity rules out all six in one box?

options.text: $(A - B) \bmod 3$: it is 1 in every row, and 0 with all six in one box
The total $A + B + C$: it is always 6
options.why: The total never changes, but six in one box also totals 6. An unchanging quantity rules a target out only if the target differs in it.

options.text: $A \bmod 2$: it never changes
options.why: Row 2 has $A = 1$ and row 3 has $A = 4$. Parity of $A$ changes.

hints.text: Compute $A - B$ for a few rows.
Rows 1 to 3 give 1, $-2$ and 4.
All three leave remainder 1 modulo 3. All six in one box gives $A - B \in \{6, -6, 0\}$, remainder 0.

feedback.correct: $(A - B) \bmod 3$ stays 1, and the target needs 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each quantity against the rows, then against $(6, 0, 0)$.

byKey.total: You picked the total. It never changes, but the target shares it, so it proves nothing here.

explain.text: A quantity no move changes is an **invariant**. $(A - B) \bmod 3$ is 1 at the start, so it is 1 forever. All six in one box needs 0, so no sequence of moves gets there.

screens.title: Prove it
screens.prose: Put the proof in order. Each line follows from the ones above it.
screens.question: Order the proof that six in one box is impossible.

lines.text: A move changes one box by $-2$ and each other box by $+1$.
$-2 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, so every box goes up by 1 modulo 3.
So $A - B$ does not change modulo 3.
With all six in one box, $A - B$ is 6, $-6$ or 0: all $\equiv 0$.
So no sequence of moves puts all six in one box.

hints.text: Start with what one move does.
The modulo 3 fact turns $-2$ and $+1$ into the same change.
Move, modulo 3, invariant; then the start's value and the target's value; then the conclusion.

feedback.correct: Effect of a move, the invariant, two values, the conclusion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The invariant must be proved before its values are compared.

explain.text: Every invariant proof has this shape: show one move cannot change the quantity, then compare start and target. Four lines settled what no amount of play could.

screens.title: Dominoes on a chessboard
screens.prose: Cut two opposite corners off a chessboard, leaving 62 squares. Can 31 dominoes cover them? Each domino covers two neighbouring squares, one shaded and one plain.
screens.question: How many shaded squares are left?

widget.accept: 30 shaded and 32 plain: both corners removed were shaded.
widget.label: Shaded squares

hints.text: What colour are the two removed corners?
Opposite corners of a chessboard have the same colour.
The board had 32 shaded squares; both corners were shaded, so 30 remain.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded squares, without the two corners.

byKey.half: 31 would be half of 62. Both removed corners were shaded, so the colours are not even.
byKey.ignore: 32 is the count before the corners were cut off.

explain.text: 31 dominoes always cover 31 shaded and 31 plain squares, whatever their layout. The board has 30 and 32, so no tiling exists. The invariant is shaded minus plain covered, which every domino leaves at 0.

screens.title: The difference game
screens.prose: The board holds 3, 5, 6 and 9. A move replaces two numbers by the absolute value of their difference. After three moves one number is left.
screens.question: What can you say about the last number before playing?

options.text: It is odd
It can be 0 with good play
options.why: You tried to cancel pairs. Every move keeps the sum's parity, and the sum 23 is odd, so 0 is impossible.

options.text: Nothing: it depends on the moves
options.why: Its value does depend on the moves: 1, 5 or 7. Its parity does not.

options.text: It is even
options.why: Replacing $x, y$ by $|x - y|$ changes the sum by $2 \min(x, y)$, an even number, so the sum stays odd.

hints.text: How does one move change the sum?
$x + y$ and $|x - y|$ differ by $2 \min(x, y)$.
So the parity of the sum never changes. $3 + 5 + 6 + 9 = 23$ is odd.

feedback.correct: Odd: the sum's parity is an invariant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the sum modulo 2 through one move.

byKey.zero: You expected a clever order to cancel everything. The sum stays odd, so the last number is odd.

explain.text: Each move changes the sum by an even amount, so the sum stays odd until one number is left. Playing every order gives 1, 5 or 7, all odd. The parity of the sum answers the question in $O(n)$.

canvas.caption: Sum 23 is odd, so the last number is odd.

screens.title: A gcd invariant
screens.prose: Start from the pair $(1, 1)$. A move replaces $(x, y)$ by $(x + y, y)$ or by $(x, x + y)$. A common divisor of $x + y$ and $y$ also divides $x$, so $\gcd$ never changes.

lines: All numbers are positive whole numbers.
params.title: The pair game

screens.question: Which pair can you reach from $(1, 1)$?

options.why: $\gcd(6, 4) = 2$, but every move keeps the gcd at $\gcd(1, 1) = 1$.
$\gcd(4, 4) = 4$, not 1. The invariant rules it out.

hints.text: Compute each pair's gcd.
Only $(7, 5)$ has gcd 1.
Walk back from $(7, 5)$: the larger number came from a sum, so subtract the smaller.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The gcd is the same in every reachable pair.

explain.text: The gcd ruled out $(6, 4)$ and $(4, 4)$. For $(7, 5)$ we walk back, each time subtracting the smaller number from the larger: $(2, 5)$, $(2, 3)$, $(2, 1)$, $(1, 1)$. The sum $x + y$ falls at every step back, a **monovariant**, so the walk must end.

lines: All numbers are positive whole numbers.

screens.title: An invariant is not a route
screens.prose: Same game, new start: $(3, 2)$. The target is $(2, 7)$. Both pairs have gcd 1.

lines: All numbers are positive whole numbers.
params.title: The pair game

screens.question: Can you reach $(2, 7)$ from $(3, 2)$?

options.why: You used the invariant as proof that a route exists. Equal gcds only fail to rule $(2, 7)$ out.

options.text: Only a search of every sequence of moves can tell
options.why: Forward search doubles with every move. The walk back is unique and short.

hints.text: Which pair could $(2, 7)$ have come from?
$7 > 2$, so the last move was $(2, 5) \to (2, 7)$.
Keep walking back: $(2, 5)$, $(2, 3)$, $(2, 1)$, $(1, 1)$. Numbers never shrink going forward, and $(3, 2)$ never appears.

feedback.correct: No. The only route into $(2, 7)$ misses $(3, 2)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Walk back from the target.

byKey.yes: You treated the matching gcd as proof. An invariant can only rule targets out; a route needs a construction.

explain.text: Each pair has one possible parent, so walking back is forced. The walk from $(2, 7)$ reaches $(1, 1)$ without meeting $(3, 2)$, and going further back is impossible. When the invariant agrees, you still need a route, or another invariant.

lines: All numbers are positive whole numbers.

screens.title: Write can_reach
screens.prose: Write `can_reach(x, y, c, d)`: can moves take $(x, y)$ to $(c, d)$? All four are whole numbers from 1 to $10^{18}$. Walk back from $(c, d)$. For speed, subtract the smaller number as many times as fit in one `%`, stopping exactly at the start when you can.

lines: c > d: the parent is (c − d, d)
c < d: the parent is (c, d − c)
c = d: no parent, unless it is the start
params.title: Walking back

screens.question: Write `can_reach(x, y, c, d)`.

widget.how: Check runs 15 hidden tests: the target equal to the start, equal numbers, gcd mismatches, a target whose walk misses the start, and pairs up to $10^{18}$. Walking back one subtraction at a time takes $10^{18}$ turns on test 11 and is stopped.

hints.text: While $c \ge x$ and $d \ge y$, step back towards the start.
If $c > d$ and $d = y$, the start is reached exactly when $(c - x)$ is a multiple of $d$.
Otherwise set `c %= d` (or `d %= c`), and stop with `False` when $c = d$ is not the start or a number drops below the start's.

feedback.correct: A Euclid-style walk: $O(\log)$ steps even at $10^{18}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing row: the start itself and equal numbers are the usual slips.

explain.text: The walk back is Euclid's algorithm on $(c, d)$, which is why it finishes in about 90 steps. It is the construction an invariant cannot give: it either finds the route or proves there is none.

screens.title: Invariants and monovariants
screens.prose:
An **invariant** is a quantity no move changes: a sum, a parity, a remainder, a gcd. A **monovariant** only rises, or only falls, which proves that a process ends.

$$I(\text{start}) \ne I(\text{target}) \implies \text{the target cannot be reached}$$

When they agree, build a route.

lines: All numbers are positive whole numbers.
params.title: The pair game

screens.question: A position's invariant matches the target's. What do you know?

options.text: Not yet whether it is reachable: build a route or find another invariant
The target is reachable
options.why: Agreement only means this invariant cannot rule it out: $(3, 2)$ and $(2, 7)$ agree, and $(2, 7)$ is out of reach.

options.text: The target is impossible
options.why: A matching invariant proves nothing either way.

feedback.correct: An invariant rules targets out; only a construction rules them in.

explain.text: The pair game used both kinds: the gcd ruled targets out, and the falling sum made the walk back end. Many contest problems marked impossible or yes-or-no hide one of these.

screens.title: Conservation in a backtest
screens.prose: A backtest logs its cash and shares after each fill. At a fill, cash plus shares times the fill price cannot change: the trade only swaps cash for shares at that price.
screens.question: Tap the line where the invariant fails.

hints.text: Value the book at the fill price just before and just after each fill.
At the sale: before, $8{,}440 + 30 \cdot 55 = 10{,}090$.
After the sale: $8{,}990 + 10 \cdot 55 = 9{,}540$. The share count should have been 20.

feedback.correct: The sale: £10,090 before and £9,540 after, at the same price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check cash plus shares times the price at each fill.

byKey.l3: At the buy, $10{,}000 = 8{,}440 + 30 \cdot 52$: the invariant holds there.
byKey.l2: The start line has no fill to check.
byKey.l1: That is the heading. Tap a fill line.

explain.text: Selling 10 of 30 shares should leave 20, giving $8{,}990 + 20 \cdot 55 = 10{,}090$. The log shows 10, so the position update subtracted twice. An assertion of this invariant after every fill catches the bug in the first test run.

ideas: An invariant is a quantity no move changes: a sum, a parity, a remainder or a gcd.
If start and target differ in an invariant, the target is impossible; if they agree, you still need a route.
A monovariant only rises or only falls, so a process that moves it must end, as the walk back in the pair game does.

formula.name: Invariant test
formula.note: The converse is false: agreement proves nothing.
